stances.claim: Critics' fear that an eight-justice (soon eleven-justice) Duterte supermajority would render the SC subservient and inutile the system of checks and balances is overdrawn -- history shows that Courts composed largely or even wholly of an incumbent president's appointees can and do speak and act independently.

Even during Cory Aquino's revolutionary regime -- when she appointed all the justices -- the Court struck down her acts and edicts; under Arroyo, who eventually named the entirety of the Court's membership during her 9.5-year tenure, the Panganiban Court (dominated by her appointees) issued landmark decisions against her wishes including Senate v. Ermita, Bayan v. Ermita, David v. GMA, and Lambino v. Comelec.

Personal-disclosure framing: 'Modesty aside, I owe her [Arroyo] my appointment as chief justice, yet the Panganiban Court... promulgated several major decisions against her wishes' -- and yet 'my personal relations with her remained cordial and friendly.'

The justices are aware that their decisions and votes are 'recorded eternally in books and other repositories from where the public, including their heirs and descendants, continuously review and rate their performance' -- this longitudinal-legacy accountability is itself a structural incentive for independence even within a presidentially-stacked Court.

notable_anecdotes: Arroyo's July 9 dinner remark in the presence of President Duterte, preserved verbatim: 'I thank you that when you became President, you provided the atmosphere in which the Court had the freedom to acquit me of the trumped-up charges of my successor and your predecessor, so that the Court voted 11-4 in my favor, including half of those who were appointed by my successor' -- used as the column's most ironic data point.

CJ's own four-decision rollcall from his term -- Senate v. Ermita (unanimous), Bayan v. Ermita (unanimous), David v. GMA (11-3), Lambino v. Comelec (8-7) -- all against Arroyo's wishes despite being decided by her appointees, anchoring the column's main thesis in first-person institutional memory.

The closing aphorism: 'The President and the Court could disagree without being disagreeable' -- a personal-relations frame echoing CJ's 'friends can differ without being difficult' line from the Carpio piece a week later.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to critics fearing that the elevation of Justice Rodil V. Zalameda -- giving President Duterte's appointees a clear majority (eight of fifteen) on the Supreme Court, with three more vacancies to come before year-end (Jardeleza on Sept 26, Bersamin on Oct 18, Carpio on Oct 26) and a new CJ slot -- will produce a subservient Court that renders the system of checks and balances 'inutile.' Critics point to the 'foreboding' decisions on the Marcos burial at Libingan ng mga Bayani and the quo warranto ouster of CJ Sereno, and to Arroyo's July 9 dinner remark crediting Duterte for 'provid[ing] the atmosphere in which the Court had the freedom to acquit me... 11-4 in my favor, including half of those who were appointed by my successor.' CJ counters with historical counter-examples: Cory Aquino's revolutionary-regime appointees still struck down her acts and edicts; and the Panganiban Court -- dominated by Arroyo appointees -- produced landmark decisions against her wishes (Senate v. Ermita, Bayan v. Ermita, David v. GMA, Lambino v. Comelec) even as his personal relations with her remained cordial. The structural reason, he argues, is that justices know their votes are 'recorded eternally in books and other repositories from where the public, including their heirs and descendants, continuously review and rate their performance,' so they remain faithful to the constitutional command of 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence -- with emphasis on independence.' The President and the Court, he closes, 'could disagree without being disagreeable.'
